newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INTERVIEW - Time right for float, says NZ's GPS.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Time right for float, says NZ's GPS.

text.p: The time is right for a float of state-owned Government Property Services, its general manager Nick Wevers said on Thursday.

Property values and rentals are on an upward curve and the investment community had signalled it would welcome flotation of GPS's 35-building portfolio, predominated by well-tenanted offices in Wellington, he said.
"Institutions are crying out for a float," Wevers told Reuters. "It would make sense to float -- better than a trade sale where there are a limited number of buyers in New Zealand."
"The board believes the best option for the crown to get the best return from the sale is a float," he said.

The company believes it is in good financial stead. It reported a net profit of NZ$23.4 million in the March year, including a revaluation gain of $6.4 million, compared with $4.1 million last year after a revaluation write-off.
Wevers said returns on assets of nine percent, projected to rise to 9.6 percent in the current year, compared more than favourably with returns from listed property companies.
Treasurer Winston Peters in last Thursday's budget said the government would study sale of GPS "by means of a public float".

Although Treasury will conduct a scoping study to examine the best means of selling GPS, other methods such as a trade sale, or selling off GPS's 35 properties singly or in groups, have been tried in the past and failed.
A contract for the sale of GPS was put the government last year but was rejected for undisclosed reasons.
Only two buildings valued over $10 million were sold in Wellington last year and GPS has 10 such properties, suggesting disposal of the portfolio would be difficult.
While institutions are overweight in property, they would prefer the liquidity of a listed company as a means of owning buildings, Wevers said.
Possibly the best alternative to a float, because of strong returns, would be for the government to retain ownership.
But Peters has said no strong policy reason exists for state ownership to continue as it exposed government to market risks.
Wevers said an IPO should value the company close to current valuation -- with the property in the books at $265.6 million and shareholders' equity at $173.3 million.

"We would hope that GPS buildings are valued close to where a float would occur at. Our values are in my view good market values and that shows through in our returns. (The returns) indicate that our values are correct," he added.
For the government a sale will still not be a windfall.
It established GPS at the peak of the 1987 property boom with GPS having to pay inflated 1987 prices for 250 properties.

Then, post crash, GPS was hit by a slump in values, rentals, a shrinking government, departments freed to leave GPS buildings, and negative cash flow. By 1992 it ran out of equity. In 1993 the government had to inject $145 million.
An investment in GPS would be very much an investment in Wellington property which comprises 82 percent of GPS's assets.
But Wevers argued that was a positive feature, saying its cluster of buildings near parliament was perfectly positioned for the 90 percent of government department tenants.
"In a sense we have one side of the Monopoly board in Wellington. We're in a strong position in our market because of the properties we've got and where there are."
He said the Wellington market was more stable than Auckland, recent growth rates were strong and vacancy rates low.
"If you look at our ability to generate cash profits with our present 67:33 gearing, it looks good for potential shareholders, or the current shareholder," Wevers said.
